chunks.text: Everything warm glows. You just can't see it.
This is DIY-Thermocam V4. A thermal camera you build yourself.
At its heart sits a FLIR Lepton.
chunks.say: At its heart sits a Fleer Lepton.

chunks.text: It has nineteen thousand two hundred pixels, and every one of them measures a temperature, from minus ten to four hundred fifty degrees.
The new V4 board comes fully assembled. No soldering.
Plug in the Lepton, the Teensy, the battery and the touchscreen. Eight screws close the shell.
Print the shell yourself, or have it cut from acrylic. Both come from the same design files.
Switch it on, and Firmware 4.0 opens straight into the live image.
The hottest spot, the coldest spot and the center, measured almost nine times a second.
Everything else is one tap away: set the range, place your own measuring spots, record photos and video, and look back in the gallery.
Find the overloaded breaker. The drafty window. The one part that runs too hot.
With the larger battery, it runs for up to six hours, and it charges over USB-C.
Plug in one cable, and DIY-Thermocam Studio shows the same image live on your computer.
Draw regions, set alarms, and export your recordings, on Mac, Windows and Linux.
All parts, including the sensor, come to just under three hundred dollars.
The board, the shell, the firmware and Studio: every file is yours to read and change.
